technicalClarifications: Kernel residency is not continuous CPU execution.
A mode switch does not necessarily cause a process switch.
The base/limit length convention uses an exclusive upper bound; an upper-address convention must be stated separately.
The single-threaded process model does not prohibit multithreaded parallel execution.
Cascading termination is an OS-dependent policy; Unix orphan reparenting is not the same as a zombie.
Threads may need kernel services for creation, blocking and synchronization despite user-space shared-memory communication.
The course uses trap/exception/software interrupt terminology broadly; architecture-specific terminology varies.
Scheduling waiting=C−A−B is used only for single-burst/no-I/O examples.
SJF optimality is stated with known bursts and appropriate availability assumptions.
Preemptive-priority ties require an explicit policy; the source example does not fully state one.
Peterson’s textbook proof requires sequentially consistent ordering; ordinary unsynchronized variables are unsafe in modern implementations.
The lecture mutex pseudocode must be interpreted as atomic acquisition, not a separate plain check and store.
Semaphores and mutexes can differ in ownership and signaling semantics.

Original PA wording is preserved after PDF formatting normalization: wrapped lines are joined, page footers removed, extraction soft-hyphen control characters removed, and the split words “W aiting” and “T erminated” repaired. Subpart labels are preserved.

The 28 answers are independently written teaching/reference answers checked against the supplied university solution documents. They are not official marking schemes or promises of exam marks. Checklists support student self-assessment; free text is not automatically graded.

PA2-03 distinguishes the mode of an initiating request/instruction from its kernel handling. PA2-04 corrects the misleading implication that a CPU cannot return to user work while I/O proceeds, and explains that interrupt return is not always a return to user mode.
PA2-05 qualifies architecture-dependent “trap” terminology and system-call entry paths. PA2-06 uses the course’s conceptual interrupt policies without claiming all real kernels permit nesting.
PA2-07 uses the source’s size interpretation of limit, yielding [4000,5200), and explicitly separates physical addresses from logical offsets.

PA2-08 does not invent a numerical allocation policy or equate CPU and GPU cores. PA2-10 preserves the key’s preferred matches while avoiding safety guarantees or treating modular/monolithic designs as mutually exclusive.

PA3-03 notes that interrupt handling need not switch processes. PA3-07 distinguishes generic creation-policy options from actual Linux fork behavior. PA3-09/10/11 clarify reaping, encoded status and the absence of universal parent-exit cascading termination.
Question PDF page locations are grounded in the extracted page footers and exercise boundaries. The alternate PA1 set duplicates PA3 and does not expand the official core count.
All 36 questions are independently authored practice, not official GIU exam items or a claim about official exam format, marks or duration.
Distribution: 16 multiple choice, 8 true/false, 6 single-choice scenarios and 6 single-choice Linux-output questions. Each has exactly one indexed correct option.
Scope follows the user clarification to include all six provided lecture PDFs by title, without inventing lecture numbering; Labs 1–3 remain the practical scope.
Every item includes a source-document topic or section. Examples and numerical values are independently prepared unless explicitly described as the course convention.
Scheduling questions state arrivals, tie conditions, CPU count, I/O and overhead assumptions to keep grading objective.
The Lab 2 exit-status sequencing error is corrected: successful cat replaces the earlier ls status. GNU Bash manual supports this correction.
Technical review checks distinguish mode changes from process switches, root credentials from kernel mode, Ready from Running, and shell Running from Linux R.
Objective question results measure performance on this bank, not a probability of passing the exam. No free-text keyword grading is included.
